column2: The T-SQL statement that defines a new table and its columns is {{c1::CREATE TABLE}}.
column3:
CREATE TABLE defines the columns that future inserts use. Each column has a type, and the definition can add rules such as NOT NULL.
Review source

column2: In an uncompressed SQL Server row, an INT value uses {{c1::4 bytes}}.
column3:
Four bytes is the value's uncompressed width. Choose INT only if both current and expected values fit its range.
Review source

column2: In an uncompressed SQL Server row, a BIGINT value uses {{c1::8 bytes}}.
column3:
BIGINT uses four more bytes per uncompressed value than INT. That extra width is useful when the required range exceeds INT.
Review source

column2: In DECIMAL(p,s), p specifies the {{c1::total number of digits}}.
column3:
Precision counts the whole value's decimal digits. With DECIMAL(10,2), the two fractional digits leave room for eight digits before the decimal point.
Review source

column2: In DECIMAL(p,s), s specifies the {{c1::number of digits after the decimal point}}.
column3:
Scale is included in precision. For example, DECIMAL(10,2) reserves two of its ten digits for the fractional portion.
Review source

column2: With row compression off, a DECIMAL(10,2) value uses {{c1::9 bytes}} of payload storage.
column3:
SQL Server groups DECIMAL storage by precision bands. A precision of 10 enters the 9-byte band even if the actual value contains fewer digits.
Review source

column2: In VARCHAR(n), n limits the string's {{c1::byte length}}.
column3:
Under UTF-8, some characters use several bytes. A VARCHAR limit therefore does not guarantee space for that many characters.
Review source

column2: SQL Server DATETIME2 supports up to {{c1::7}} fractional-second digits.
column3:
Seven digits describe the finest representable fractional precision. A data source or clock can still supply less accurate timestamps.
Review source

column2: SQL Server's document-oriented data type for XML content is {{c1::XML}}.
column3:
An XML column supports XML-aware validation and queries. A text column stores characters without treating them as XML.
Review source

column2: In SQL Server 2025, the native JSON data type stores documents in a {{c1::binary format}}.
column3:
The engine stores parsed documents in the native type. It can read a property without reparsing the original text for every lookup.
Review source

column2: A SQL Server UNIQUEIDENTIFIER value uses {{c1::16 bytes}}.
column3:
A GUID takes 16 bytes, compared with four for INT. Consider that difference if the value will be copied into other index entries.
Review source

column2: In SQL Server, IDENTITY(100,5) has an initial seed of {{c1::100}}.
column3:
On a new table, the first generated value is normally the seed of 100. The second argument controls how far the generator advances.
Review source

column2: In SQL Server, IDENTITY(100,5) has an increment of {{c1::5}}.
column3:
Starting at 100, the ordinary generated series advances to 105 and then 110. Gaps can still occur if values are consumed but not stored.
Review source

column2: A SQL Server identity column still needs a PRIMARY KEY or UNIQUE rule to enforce {{c1::uniqueness}}.
column3:
IDENTITY generates values, but a separate key or unique constraint enforces the stored result. This matters when values can be inserted or reseeded outside normal generation.
Review source

column2: A DATETIME2 column can use DEFAULT ({{c1::SYSUTCDATETIME()}}) for a current UTC insertion timestamp.
column3:
The default fills in a UTC value when an insert omits the column. It does not update a timestamp that is already stored.
Review source

column2: In analytical modeling, a {{c1::fact table}} stores measurable events.
column3:
A sales fact row can store quantities and amounts for one recorded event. Dimension keys connect those measures to descriptive details.
Review source

column2: In analytical modeling, a {{c1::dimension table}} provides descriptive context for measured events.
column3:
A Product dimension can describe category and brand. Those details let an analyst group measures from the fact table without storing every description on each fact row.
Review source

column2: Given Quantity INT NOT NULL DEFAULT (0), an INSERT that omits Quantity receives {{c1::0}}.
column3:
The insert omits Quantity, so SQL Server uses the default. An explicit NULL would instead violate this column's NOT NULL rule.
Review source
